essays.stem: A catering business keeps its receipts in a shoebox and pays bills from the owner's personal account. Plan how you would set up an organised financial record system for it.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would open a separate business bank account and arrange for all sales income to be paid into it and all business bills to be paid from it. The owner would pay herself through recorded drawings, not by mixing accounts. Next I would set up a simple bookkeeping system, preferably accounting software, with a chart of accounts suited to catering: sales, food costs, wages, transport, rent, utilities and equipment. Every transaction would be backed by a source document: sales invoices and receipts for income, supplier invoices and receipts for costs, and signed vouchers for a small imprest petty cash float. Documents would be filed each week by month and type, scanned as a backup, and kept for the period the tax and company law require. I would add a monthly routine: enter all documents, reconcile the bank account, check who owes money and who must be paid, and review cash. Finally, the owner would agree with an accountant which tax returns apply and set up a calendar of due dates.
markingPoints: Separate business bank account; owner's withdrawals recorded as drawings
Bookkeeping system or software with a suitable chart of accounts
Source documents for every transaction, including petty cash vouchers
Filing, backup and retention for the required period
Monthly routine (record, reconcile, debtors, creditors, cash) and tax calendar with an accountant

essays.stem: Explain why a profitable business can still run out of cash, and describe how a cash flow forecast helps the owner to avoid this.
essays.modelAnswer: Profit and cash are not the same. Profit is counted when a sale is made, but if the customer has 30 or 60 days to pay, the cash arrives later. Meanwhile, the business may have to pay suppliers, wages and rent straight away. Cash also goes into stock that has not yet sold, into loan repayments, into new equipment and into the owner's drawings, none of which reduce profit in the same way. A fast-growing business is at special risk, because it buys more stock and takes on more staff before customers pay. A cash flow forecast lists, month by month, the cash expected in from sales, loans and other sources, and the cash expected out for every payment, with opening and closing balances. It shows in advance any month where cash will fall below zero or below a safe level. The owner can then act early: chase debtors, ask suppliers for longer terms, delay a purchase, arrange an overdraft, or reduce drawings. The forecast should be updated monthly with actual figures.
markingPoints: Explains the difference between profit and cash (timing of receipts and payments)
Names other cash drains: stock, loan repayments, equipment, drawings, growth
Describes the forecast: receipts, payments, opening and closing balances by month
Shows how it reveals shortfalls in advance
Gives actions the owner can take and the need to update monthly

essays.stem: Describe a credit control procedure for a small business that sells to other firms on 30-day terms.
essays.modelAnswer: Credit control starts before the sale. A new customer should complete a credit application, and the business should check trade references and set a credit limit. The terms, 30 days from the invoice date, should be agreed in writing. Invoices must go out promptly and correctly, with the due date, the TRN and payment details clearly shown, since errors give customers a reason to delay. Each week, an aged debtors report shows who owes what and for how long. A few days before the due date, a polite reminder can be sent to large accounts. If payment is late, the business sends a reminder at once, then telephones the customer's accounts officer to find out why and agree a date. At 45 or 60 days, a firmer letter is sent and further supplies may be put on hold until the account is settled. As a last resort, the business may use a collection agency or legal action, after taking advice. Good customers who pay on time can be rewarded with better terms.
markingPoints: Checks before giving credit: application, references, credit limit, written terms
Prompt, accurate invoices with due date and payment details
Weekly aged debtors report and reminders before or at the due date
Escalating steps for late payers: call, firmer letter, hold supplies
Last resort: collection agency or legal action after advice

essays.stem: Explain the main tax and statutory obligations a small employer in Jamaica must organise, and how the owner can keep on top of them.
essays.modelAnswer: The business must be registered with Tax Administration Jamaica and use its Taxpayer Registration Number on all tax dealings. It must keep proper records and file income tax returns on its profits each year. If its sales are above the threshold for General Consumption Tax, or it chooses to register, it must charge GCT at the current rate, keep invoices, file GCT returns and pay over the tax by the due dates, claiming back allowable input tax. As an employer, it must deduct PAYE income tax, NIS, NHT and Education Tax from employees' pay, add the employer's own contributions, including the HEART/NSTA Trust contribution where it applies, and pay them over with the required returns. It must also give employees their payslips and year-end certificates. To keep on top of this, the owner should set up a tax calendar with all due dates and reminders, use payroll and accounting software, reconcile the payroll each month, keep all records for the required period, and agree a yearly review with an accountant. She should check current rates and thresholds with the tax authority rather than relying on memory.
markingPoints: Registration with the tax authority and use of the TRN; yearly income tax returns
GCT: charge at the current rate if registered, file returns, pay over, claim input tax
Payroll deductions (PAYE, NIS, NHT, Education Tax) plus employer contributions, paid over with returns
Payslips, year-end certificates and record keeping
Tax calendar, software, monthly reconciliation and professional advice; check current rates

essays.stem: Describe the steps of a monthly bank reconciliation and explain why it matters.
essays.modelAnswer: At the end of the month, the bookkeeper gets the bank statement and the cash book for the same period. She ticks off each item that appears in both. Items on the bank statement but not in the cash book, such as bank charges, interest, direct debits or customer transfers, are checked and then entered in the cash book, giving a corrected cash book balance. Items in the cash book but not yet on the statement are listed: unpresented cheques, which are taken off the bank balance, and deposits not yet credited, which are added to it. The adjusted bank balance should now agree with the corrected cash book balance. Any difference left must be investigated, as it may be an error or a missing transaction. The reconciliation is signed and dated by the person who prepared it and reviewed by another person. It matters because it proves the cash records are complete and accurate, catches bank and recording errors quickly, can reveal fraud or theft, and gives the owner a reliable cash figure for decisions.
markingPoints: Compares the bank statement with the cash book and ticks matching items
Enters bank-only items (charges, interest, direct debits) to correct the cash book
Adjusts for unpresented cheques and deposits not yet credited
Investigates any remaining difference; prepared and reviewed by different people
Explains why it matters: accuracy, error and fraud detection, reliable cash figure

essays.stem: A firm's figures for the year are: sales J$3,000,000; cost of goods sold J$1,950,000; expenses J$720,000; current assets J$800,000; current liabilities J$500,000. Calculate the gross profit margin, the net profit and the current ratio, and comment on what they show.
essays.modelAnswer: Gross profit is sales less cost of goods sold: J$3,000,000 minus J$1,950,000 equals J$1,050,000. The gross profit margin is J$1,050,000 divided by J$3,000,000, which is 0.35, or 35%. Net profit is gross profit less expenses: J$1,050,000 minus J$720,000 equals J$330,000, which is 11% of sales. The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities: J$800,000 divided by J$500,000 equals 1.6 : 1. These figures show a business that is profitable, keeping 35 cents of every dollar of sales after the cost of goods, and 11 cents after all expenses. Whether this is good depends on the firm's past results and on similar businesses, so the owner should compare them. Expenses take up a large share of gross profit, so they are worth reviewing. A current ratio of 1.6 : 1 means it has J$1.60 of short-term assets for each J$1 of short-term debts, which is usually comfortable, though the owner should check how much of the current assets is slow-moving stock or overdue debts.
markingPoints: Gross profit J$1,050,000 and margin 35%
Net profit J$330,000 (about 11% of sales)
Current ratio 1.6 : 1
Comments sensibly on profitability and the need for comparison
Comments on liquidity and what makes up current assets

essays.stem: Compare an overdraft, a term loan and bringing in an investor as ways to fund a small business. Recommend one for buying a J$5,000,000 delivery truck.
essays.modelAnswer: An overdraft lets the business draw more than it has in its current account up to an agreed limit. It is flexible and interest is paid only on what is used, but rates are often high and the bank can reduce or withdraw it at short notice, so it suits short-term gaps in cash flow, not long-term assets. A term loan provides a lump sum repaid in fixed instalments over an agreed period, often with the asset as security. Repayments are predictable and the owner keeps full ownership, but interest must be paid whether trading is good or bad. Bringing in an investor provides equity: money in exchange for a share of the business. There are no fixed repayments and the investor may bring skills and contacts, but the owner gives up part of the profit and some control. For a J$5,000,000 truck that will earn income for several years, I recommend a term loan or asset finance such as hire purchase, matched to the truck's working life. This keeps ownership with the owner, and the truck's earnings can cover the repayments, provided the cash flow forecast shows they are affordable.
markingPoints: Overdraft: flexible but costly and can be withdrawn; suits short-term needs
Term loan: lump sum, fixed repayments, ownership kept, interest always due
Investor/equity: no fixed repayments, brings skills, but shares profit and control
Recommends a term loan or asset finance for the truck, matched to its working life
Checks affordability with a cash flow forecast

essays.stem: Evaluate the internal controls a small business with three office staff can use to protect its cash.
essays.modelAnswer: Full separation of duties is hard with only three staff, but it can be partly achieved. The person who receives cash and records sales should not also do the bank reconciliation; the owner or another staff member should. Cheques and online payments should need two approvals, or at least the owner's approval, and supporting invoices should be checked before payment. Cash takings should be counted by two people, recorded and banked daily, rather than kept on the premises. Petty cash should run on an imprest system with signed vouchers and receipts, counted by surprise from time to time. Online banking passwords must be personal and never shared, and access to the accounting software should be set by role. A monthly review by the owner of the bank reconciliation, aged debtors and unusual payments is one of the strongest controls in a small firm, because staff know someone checks. Rotating duties and requiring staff to take their leave can bring hidden problems to light. No control is perfect, so the cost of each must be weighed against the risk, but these simple steps greatly reduce the chance of error or theft.
markingPoints: Separation of duties as far as possible (receiving vs recording vs reconciling)
Approvals for payments, checked against invoices
Daily banking, two-person counts, imprest petty cash
Password and software access controls
Owner's monthly review, rotation and leave; weighs cost against risk

essays.stem: Compare manual books with accounting software for a small business, and recommend which a growing hardware store in Mandeville should use.
essays.modelAnswer: Manual books, such as a cash book, sales and purchase records kept on paper or a simple spreadsheet, are cheap and easy to start, and need no special skills or equipment. However, they are slow, every total must be added by hand, mistakes are easy to make and hard to find, and reports such as a profit statement or aged debtors list take a long time to prepare. They can also be lost or damaged. Accounting software costs money for the licence or subscription and needs training, a computer and regular backups. In return it records transactions quickly, posts both sides of each entry automatically, keeps running totals, and produces up-to-date reports at the press of a button. Many packages handle invoicing, stock, GCT and payroll, and can link to the bank. A growing hardware store has many stock items, credit customers and suppliers, and must manage GCT and payroll. I recommend accounting software with a stock module, with staff trained to use it, user access set by role, and daily backups to a secure second place.
markingPoints: Manual: low cost and simple, but slow, error-prone, slow reports, risk of loss
Software: cost and training needed, but fast, accurate and gives current reports
Notes useful features (invoicing, stock, GCT, payroll, bank links)
Recommends software for the growing hardware store, with reasons linked to its needs
Includes training, access control and backups

essays.stem: Justify a monthly financial routine for a small business owner, and explain when she should seek professional advice.
essays.modelAnswer: A fixed monthly routine turns finance from a crisis into a habit. In the first week of each month, the owner or bookkeeper should enter all of last month's invoices, receipts and payroll so that the records are complete. Next, the bank account and petty cash should be reconciled, so she knows the true cash position and can spot errors early. She should then review the aged debtors list and chase overdue accounts, and list the bills and statutory payments due in the month ahead, paying on time to avoid penalties and keep supplier goodwill. Comparing the month's income and costs with the budget or the same month last year shows trends while there is still time to act. Finally, she should update the cash flow forecast for the next three to six months. This routine takes a few hours, but it gives early warning of problems and supports better decisions. She should seek an accountant's advice when setting up the system, at year end, on tax questions, before borrowing or taking on an investor, when hiring staff for the first time, and whenever the figures show something she does not understand.
markingPoints: Enters all documents each month so records are complete
Reconciles bank and petty cash for a true cash position
Reviews debtors and upcoming payments, including statutory ones
Compares results with budget or last year and updates the cash flow forecast
Names sensible times to seek professional advice

practical1.title: Organise one month of a small business's financial records
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a pack of documents for one month of a made-up small business (for example a print shop in Spanish Town): sales invoices, supplier invoices, receipts, petty cash vouchers, a payroll summary and a bank statement. As a group, organise and record them. Give each member a named role: cash book keeper (enters all bank receipts and payments in a spreadsheet cash book), petty cash officer (runs the imprest float and restores it at month end), debtors and creditors officer (prepares an aged debtors list and a list of bills due), bank reconciliation lead (prepares the reconciliation statement), and controller (files the documents, checks every total twice and signs off the work). In a group of four, the controller also does the filing. Photograph or screenshot each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Document pack from the assessor (invoices, receipts, vouchers, payroll summary, bank statement)
Box files or folders, dividers and labels
Printed blank templates for petty cash, cash book and reconciliation (optional)
photos: The documents sorted and filed by type and date, with labelled dividers
The spreadsheet cash book with opening and closing balances
The petty cash record and the restoring amount
The aged debtors list and the list of bills due
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the records
Entered each transaction from the correct source document, with dates and references
Totals and balances are correct and were checked twice
Petty cash was restored to the float with the correct amount
Bank reconciliation agrees, with unpresented cheques and uncredited deposits listed
Aged debtors list and bills due are accurate and in a clear format
Filing is orderly and the controller signed off the final work
safety: Treat the document pack as confidential financial information; leave all copies with the assessor
Use made-up names and figures only; do not bring in any real bank or personal details
Lock or log off computers when you step away
Take short screen breaks and sit comfortably

practical2.title: Prepare a six-month cash flow forecast and finance plan
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group the details of a made-up business planning to grow (for example a juice maker in St Elizabeth that has won a supermarket order). As a group, prepare a six-month cash flow forecast in a spreadsheet, find any month where cash falls below a safe level, and recommend how to deal with it. Give each member a named role: receipts lead (sales and timing of customer payments), payments lead (suppliers, wages, rent and loan repayments), statutory and tax lead (builds a calendar of GCT, PAYE and other statutory payments; uses 'at the current rate' and the figures given, inventing no rates), finance options lead (compares an overdraft, a term loan and an investor), and editor (writes the one-page finance plan and checks every formula and total). In a group of four, the editor also checks the statutory calendar. Photograph or screenshot each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Business details and figures from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet software and a printer
photos: The group's list of assumptions on the flipchart
The cash flow forecast on screen with the formulas showing
The month or months of shortfall highlighted
The statutory and tax payment calendar
The one-page finance plan with the recommendation
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the forecast or plan
Placed receipts and payments in the right months, taking credit terms into account
Formulas and closing balances are correct and checked twice
Statutory calendar shows the payments and due dates given, with no invented rates
Compared finance options fairly and gave a justified recommendation
Finance plan is clear, professional and fits on one page
safety: Use only the made-up figures given; keep the group's work confidential
Do not share login details; save work to the Centre's own folder
Agree a fair share of the work and realistic time limits
Take short breaks from the screen
